## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | The Nalu, also called Nalo, Nanum, or Nanu, are a West African ethnic group. |
| Where | Guinea and Guinea-Bissau, especially along the coast, north of the Nuñez River, on the Tristão islands, around Kanfarandé, and in the Cacine estuary. |
| How many | About 10,000 to 25,000 speakers; Wilson reports around 12,000. |
| Language | Nalu, an endangered Atlantic language with six dialects. |
| Religion | Not documented; the Simo is a secret society active among the Nalu and related groups. |
| Known for | Coastal settlements in Guinea and Guinea-Bissau · The endangered Nalu language · The Simo secret society · Crocodile-shaped wooden masks · Baskets, fish-traps, and oyster-gathering tools |

## Overview

The Nalu are a West African people living mainly along the coasts of Guinea and Guinea-Bissau. They settled in the region before the Mandé or Mandinka peoples and have been described as “pre-Mandingas.” Their language is endangered, with speakers shifting toward Susu in Guinea. Sources document a small group of everyday objects and a crocodile-shaped wooden mask, but give little information about clothing, buildings, music, rituals, or stories.

## Material culture

The documented material culture includes fibre baskets, wooden and iron tools, a bamboo fish-trap, a stool, and a crocodile-shaped wooden mask.

### Textile & pattern traditions

- **Crocodile mask imagery** — A wooden mask shows a crocodile with two long horns and white painted decorations along the top of its snout.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum records document baskets, a stool, an oyster-gathering tool, and a fish-trap.

- **Fibre basket** — This basket is made from vegetable fibre, straw, bamboo, and cotton cloth.
- **Wooden stool** — The stool is made of wood.
- **Oyster-gathering tool** — This iron-and-wood tool is used to knock oysters off mangrove roots.
- **Bamboo fish-trap** — The fish-trap is made of bamboo.
- **Storage basket** — The storage basket is made from vegetable fibre, straw, and bamboo.

## Music & performance

The sources name the Simo secret society.

- **Simo secret society** (*Simo*) — The Simo is a West African secret society active among the Nalu and related groups.
- **Crocodile mask** — A wooden mask has two long horns, white painted decorations, and a fringe of grass along its bottom edge.

## Dance & theatre

- **Crocodile-shaped wooden mask** — The mask has two long horns, white painted decorations, and a grass fringe, but its use is not explained.

## Festivals & rituals

- **Simo society** (*Simo*) — The Simo is identified as a secret society, but its rites and calendar are not described.

## Foodways

- **Oyster-gathering tool** — An iron-and-wood tool is used to knock oysters from mangrove roots.

## Language & religion

Nalu is an endangered Atlantic language spoken mainly by adults, while Nalu religious beliefs are not documented.

- **Nalu language** (*Nalu*) — Nalu, also called Nalou, nalɛ, or nul, has six dialects and is spoken in Guinea and Guinea-Bissau.
- **Nalu language variants** (*Nalou*) — Nalou is another spelling of the Nalu language.
- **Nalu language variant** (*nalɛ*) — nalɛ is another name for the Nalu language.
- **Nalu language variant** (*nul*) — nul is another name for the Nalu language.
- **Shift toward Susu** (*Susu*) — Nalu speakers in Guinea are shifting toward Susu, although the language continues in a few remote villages around Katoufoura.

## Glossary

- *Nalu* — The people and their language
- *Nalo* — Another name for the Nalu
- *Nanum* — Another name for the Nalu
- *Nanu* — Another name for the Nalu
- *Nalou* — Another name for the Nalu language
- *nalɛ* — Another name for the Nalu language
- *nul* — Another name for the Nalu language
- *Simo* — A secret society
- *Susu* — A language Nalu speakers are shifting toward

## Sources & further reading

- “Nalu people,” *Wikipedia*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nalu_people
- “Nalu language,” *Wikipedia*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nalu_language
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: the supplied UNESCO material lists no inscriptions for Guinea concerning the Nalu.
- British Museum catalogue records supplied for the basket, stool, oyster-gathering tool, fish-trap, storage basket, crocodile mask, and painted wooden bird figure.
